blocks.text: A strain gauge glued to a bridge hanger is a thin foil grid that stretches with the steel beneath it, and it can detect a change in length of about one part in a million. That tiny ratio, not the stretch in millimetres, is what engineers record, because it lets one measurement describe members of any size.

blocks.markdown: **Normal strain** measures how much a line element stretches or shortens relative to its original length. If a gauge length $L_0$ becomes $L_0+\delta$, the average normal strain is $\varepsilon = \delta/L_0$. Strain is a dimensionless ratio; it is often quoted in microstrain ($\mu\varepsilon = 10^{-6}$) or as a percentage. Extension is positive, shortening negative.

blocks.title: Shear strain
blocks.text: **Shear strain** $\gamma$ is the change in the right angle between two initially perpendicular line elements, measured in radians. It describes distortion of shape rather than change of length. For small angles $\gamma \approx \tan\gamma$ equals the sideways displacement divided by the height of the element.

blocks.caption: Hooke's law for a linear elastic isotropic material; $E$ = Young's modulus, $G$ = shear modulus, $\nu$ = Poisson's ratio.

blocks.title: Strain of a stretched wire
blocks.prompt: A steel wire of original length 2.500 m is found to be 2.5032 m long under load. Find the normal strain.

steps.text: Divide by the original length (same units).

blocks.answer: The strain is 1.28 x 10^-3 (1280 microstrain, or 0.128 %).

blocks.markdown: **Hooke's law.** For many materials, below the proportional limit, stress is proportional to strain: $\sigma = E\varepsilon$. Combining it with $\sigma = P/A$ and $\varepsilon = \delta/L$ gives the elongation of a uniform bar, $\delta = PL/(AE)$. The law holds only while the material remains linear elastic; beyond yield, unloading leaves a permanent strain.

blocks.title: Elongation of a steel bar
blocks.prompt: A steel bar (E = 200 GPa) of diameter 20 mm and length 1.5 m carries a tensile load of 45 kN. Find the stress, strain and elongation.

steps.text: Strain from Hooke's law, E = 200 000 MPa.

blocks.answer: The bar carries 143 MPa and stretches by about 1.07 mm, well within the elastic range of structural steel.

blocks.caption: Typical elastic constants; use given data in calculations

blocks.markdown: **Shear and the shear modulus.** A shear stress $\tau$ distorts an element; within the elastic range $\tau = G\gamma$. A rubber bearing pad between a bridge girder and its pier is a familiar example: the top moves sideways relative to the bottom by $\gamma t$, where $t$ is the pad thickness.

blocks.title: Shear deformation of an elastomeric pad
blocks.prompt: A rubber pad (G = 0.9 MPa) has plan area 50 000 mm^2 and thickness 25 mm. A horizontal force of 18 kN is applied to its top face while the bottom is fixed. Find the shear strain and the horizontal movement of the top.

steps.text: Shear strain from tau = G gamma.
Horizontal movement (small-angle approximation is rough here, but rubber pads are normally designed with gamma well below this).

blocks.answer: Shear strain is 0.40 and the top moves 10 mm horizontally.

blocks.title: Units and signs
blocks.text: Keep strain dimensionless: mm/mm, not mm. Use consistent units: N, mm and MPa give elongations in mm. Hooke's law is an empirical relation for the elastic range only. For metals G is about E/2.6, so the shear modulus is always smaller than E.

points: Normal strain is change in length divided by original length (dimensionless); shear strain is the change in a right angle in radians.
Hooke's law in one dimension: sigma = E epsilon, giving delta = PL/(AE) for a uniform bar in its elastic range.
In shear tau = G gamma, with G = E/(2(1+nu)) for an isotropic material.

questions.stem: A normal strain of 0.002 in a bar is equivalent to which of the following?

options.text: 2 mm extension for every metre of length

questions.correctOptionText: 2 mm extension for every metre of length

distractorRationale.a: Correct: 0.002 x 1000 mm = 2 mm per metre.
distractorRationale.b: Treats strain as a length in mm instead of mm per mm.
distractorRationale.c: Off by a factor of ten.
distractorRationale.d: Off by a factor of ten in the other direction.

questions.explanation: Strain is extension divided by original length, so 0.002 means 0.002 mm per mm, or 2 mm per 1000 mm. It is also 0.2 percent.

questions.stem: Hooke's law, sigma = E epsilon, applies to a metal bar only if:

options.text: The bar has never been loaded before
The bar is in compression only
The stress remains below the proportional limit

questions.correctOptionText: The stress remains below the proportional limit

distractorRationale.a: Previous loading history is irrelevant within the elastic range.
distractorRationale.b: Large strains typically mean the material has yielded.
distractorRationale.c: Hooke's law applies in both tension and compression.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: linear relation holds only up to the proportional limit.

questions.explanation: Stress is proportional to strain only in the initial linear part of the stress-strain curve. Beyond the proportional limit and yield, the relationship is non-linear and unloading is not recovered.

questions.stem: Two bars have identical lengths and cross-sections and carry the same tensile force. One is steel (E = 200 GPa) and the other aluminium (E = 70 GPa). The ratio of aluminium elongation to steel elongation is about:

distractorRationale.a: Inverted: the more compliant material stretches more.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: delta is inversely proportional to E, so ratio is 200/70.
distractorRationale.c: Stress is the same, but strain differs by the modulus ratio.
distractorRationale.d: Squares the ratio, which has no basis.

questions.explanation: With the same P, L and A, delta = PL/(AE) is proportional to 1/E. The aluminium therefore stretches 200/70 = 2.86 times as much as steel.

questions.stem: A steel has E = 200 GPa and Poisson's ratio 0.30. Which value of shear modulus is consistent with G = E/(2(1+nu))?

distractorRationale.a: Uses E/3 which would be 2(1+0.5)=3 for nu = 0.5.
distractorRationale.d: Divides by 1.3 only, forgetting the factor 2.

questions.explanation: Substituting gives G = 200/(2 x 1.30) = 76.9 GPa. Because 2(1+nu) is between 2 and 3, G always lies between E/3 and E/2.

questions.stem: True or false: shear strain is the change in the angle between two line elements that were originally perpendicular, expressed in radians.
questions.explanation: That is the definition of shear strain, a measure of angular distortion. It is dimensionless, like normal strain.

questions.stem: A concrete column 2.4 m long is shortened by 1.8 mm under load. Find the normal strain in microstrain, with compression taken as negative.
questions.explanation: epsilon = -1.8/2400 = -7.5e-4, which is -750 microstrain. The negative sign records shortening.

questions.stem: An aluminium bar (E = 70 GPa) of diameter 12 mm and length 800 mm carries a tensile load of 20 kN. Find its elongation in mm.
A steel plate has E = 210 GPa and Poisson's ratio 0.30. Using the relation between E, nu and G, find the shear strain in milliradians produced by a shear stress of 50 MPa.
questions.explanation: G = 210/(2 x 1.3) = 80.77 GPa. gamma = tau/G = 50/80 770 = 6.19e-4 rad = 0.619 milliradians.

questions.stem: Starting from sigma = P/A and sigma = E epsilon, derive the elongation of a uniform bar under an axial load and state the assumptions behind it.
markingGuide: Writes sigma = P/A and epsilon = delta/L
Substitutes into sigma = E epsilon to obtain delta = PL/(AE)
States linear elastic material (below proportional limit)
States uniform cross-section and load through centroid
States small strains or that P is constant along the bar
questions.explanation: Replacing stress and strain by their definitions turns Hooke's law into a force-deformation relation. AE/L plays the role of an axial stiffness.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between normal strain and shear strain, and why a material needs a shear modulus G in addition to E. Describe how G relates to E for an isotropic material.
markingGuide: Normal strain is change of length per original length; shear strain is angular distortion of an originally right angle
Notes that tau acts parallel to a face and causes distortion, so tau = G gamma
Explains that G is a separate elastic constant describing shear response
States G = E/(2(1+nu)) for isotropic materials
Notes that only two of E, G and nu are independent
questions.explanation: Normal stress causes length change and shear stress causes angle change, so both responses need a modulus. For an isotropic material they are linked through Poisson's ratio, leaving only two independent constants.
